claims.text: Resistance to simultaneous wear and corrosion in passivity-enhanced high-entropy alloys is governed by a mechanically robust, self-healing oxide film.
Rapid repair of wear-induced film damage prevents localized corrosion.
Self-healing of the passive film decouples synergistic wear-corrosion degradation.
The baseline is an equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy.
The intervention alloy contains Mo and Al additions intended to promote a stable Cr/Mo/Al-rich passive oxide film.
Both alloy variants will be compared under simultaneous reciprocating sliding and electrochemical polarization in 3.5% NaCl.
Testing will use a 2 N load, 5 Hz sliding frequency, 25°C temperature, and polarization from -250 mV to +250 mV versus Ag/AgCl.
The relevant structural mediator is a continuously forming, mechanically adherent passive film rich in Cr, Mo, and Al oxides.
The passive film self-renews after mechanical damage.
Under combined mechanical and corrosive stress, the enhanced alloy's passive film undergoes controlled micro-fracture.
Exposure to the corrosive environment produces rapid repair of the micro-fractured passive film.
Rapid film repair prevents prolonged exposure of the underlying metal.
At moderate loads, passive-film repair can keep pace with mechanical damage.
When loading exceeds the film's fracture-toughness limit, the benefit of enhanced passivity diminishes.
Under moderate loads, the passivity-enhanced alloy will have lower wear mass loss than the baseline alloy.
Under moderate loads, the passivity-enhanced alloy will exhibit a more positive corrosion potential than the baseline alloy.
Under moderate loads, the passivity-enhanced alloy will exhibit a lower anodic current density than the baseline alloy.
At excessive load, the enhanced alloy's performance will approach that of the baseline.
Changes in bulk mechanical properties caused by Mo/Al additions may dominate degradation and eliminate the proposed passivity advantage.
Failure to observe statistically significant metric improvements or a distinct self-healing film under moderate loads would falsify the proposed mechanism.
